Clinical outcomes of hysterectomy after definitive radiotherapy for cervical cancer: a retrospective case series of 21 patients
abstractText: Abstract Objective To analyze the clinical and treatment characteristics of cervical cancer patients undergoing hysterectomy after definitive radiotherapy. Methods A retrospective study was conducted on cervical cancer patients who received hysterectomy after definitive radiotherapy at Beijing Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital from January 1, 2009 to December 31, 2024, with follow-up until November 30, 2025. Results Among 6,045 patients receiving definitive radiotherapy, 21 (0.35%) underwent subsequent hysterectomy (median age 52 years, IQR 41–59). Indications included local recurrence (14/21, 66.7%), post-radiotherapy persistence (6/21, 28.5%), and symptom-directed surgery (1/21, 4.8%). Surgical procedures: radical total hysterectomy (16 cases) and extrafascial total hysterectomy (5 cases). Among the 20 patients with confirmed persistent or recurrent malignant tissue, R0 microscopic negative margins were achieved in 16 (80.0%); the remaining 4 patients had R1 (microscopically positive) margins. The single symptom-directed patient (Patient #20, pathological complete response) achieved R0 margins and is reported separately. Median postoperative overall survival was 58.0 months (range 11–165) for the recurrence group versus 55.0 months (range 8–85) for the persistence group (log-rank p = 0.387). Patients with post-radiotherapy persistence showed poor outcomes regardless of surgery. Postoperative complications occurred in 2 of 21 patients (9.5%); the small number of events precludes reliable assessment of the association between surgical timing and complications. Conclusion In this descriptive case series, salvage hysterectomy achieved R0 resection in the majority of patients with confirmed malignant tissue despite radiation-induced pelvic fibrosis, whereas the single symptom-directed case showed a pathological complete response. Patients with local recurrence after complete remission had a numerically longer median postoperative overall survival than those with post-radiotherapy persistence, but the difference was not statistically significant. The small sample size and marked histologic imbalance between the groups preclude excluding a true clinical difference; the observed pattern is consistent with tumor biology and radiosensitivity rather than surgical timing or completeness of resection alone. These observations are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger prospective studies.

title: Benchmarking heart failure care: the ANZACS-QI Heart Failure Registry Pilot implementation and results (ANZACS-QI 86)
abstractText: aims: Heart failure is a major healthcare problem in Aotearoa New Zealand. As therapies advance and become increasingly complex it is essential that we systematically characterise phenotype and monitor adherence to relevant guidelines to drive quality improvement. Here we report the results of the ANZACS-QI Heart Failure Registry Pilot, implemented in Northern Region hospitals. methods: Age-stratified random sampling was used to identify a representative cohort of patients hospitalised with heart failure (2022 and 2023) using national administrative datasets. The electronic clinical records were reviewed and data entered into the web-based registry. Pre-specified outcomes that were analysed included rates of left ventricular assessment (left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF]) and prescription of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). results: The cohort comprised 328 patients and registry form completion rates were high (98%). LVEF assessment rates within 2 years of the index hospital discharge were 81%. Of those with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction that survived until discharge (n=137), only 13 (9%) met the composite medication indicator of being prescribed (or with documented contraindication/intolerance) all four GDMT classes. This was largely driven by 92 (67%) being ineligible for subsidy for sodium glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors; however, prescription rates of the other GDMT classes were suboptimal. conclusions: Our study highlights that there is a considerable gap between guideline recommendations and real-world practice. Following pilot completion, performance indicators have been established and the registry has expanded with the goal for it to become national. The successful implementation of the registry is an important step in quality improvement for patients hospitalised with heart failure.

title: Applying the Special Cases Concerning Cinematographic Works to Everyday Collaborative Video Production: Interpretation and Limits
Comfort, stretch, panic: Managing affect to support creative learning in complex problem-solving
abstractText: Universities are increasingly encouraged to engage students with complex real-world problems, such as those characterised by the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (Schmitz et al., 2026). Doing so leverages their emerging disciplinary knowledge and requires the development of broader competencies that are relevant to industry and other non-academic contexts (Brundiers et al., 2021). However, confronting real-world problems can be a more intimidating and emotionally charged learning process than disciplinarily bounded or pre-prepared case study work. These problems lack clear boundaries, have rich but always-incomplete information available to characterise them, are dynamic, and students may feel directly entangled with them via their everyday lives (Veltman et al., 2021; Wickson et al., 2025). Addressing complex problems requires inner transformation by educators and students to align their emerging skills and externally oriented knowledge development (Ives et al., 2023; Stein, 2021). When engaging in real-world-problem inquiry, digital tools including web search, databases and GenAI make massive quantities of information available. However, quantity is not necessarily paired with credibility, quality, and contextual relevance, and this amplification and ease of access may paradoxically increase student uncertainty and undermine creative confidence (Jose et al., 2025). This digitally-broadened information landscape, when combined with the inherent complexity of real-world problems, can trigger feelings of anxiety, disengagement or lower motivation, placing strain on classroom relationships, such as educator–student and team connections, and requiring strategic educator management. This poster will share preliminary results from a practice-led doctoral study framed by the research question: How can an educator creatively manage affect in a learning environment to support students’ creative development? The research draws data from two iterations of a 60-student interdisciplinary master’s unit at a large Australian university. In the unit, students work to create innovative projects to address local real-world systemic problems, with significant openness in the boundaries of the brief and range of solution options framed as viable. The presentation will share highlights of a reflexive thematic analysis of students’ short, written reflections on affective experience during the solution prototyping and final proposal stages of the creative process. Students experienced strong but mixed emotions, which temporally varied at an individual level and were often held simultaneously. For example, during prototyping, students commonly reported experiencing feelings such as frustration or uncertainty, and at the same time, pride or confidence – that is, positive and negative affect coexisted within individual students, and the cohort, simultaneously. These complex affective dynamics required careful educator management to encourage student progress. The poster will then feature an emerging typology, with examples, of human-centred teaching strategies deployed to support and enable students to work with and reflect on their emotional responses while seeking to creatively express ideas. These strategies ranged from whole-of-class, to small-group, to peer-to-peer, and student-to-GenAI approaches. Educator-researcher evaluations of the efficacy of these strategies will be offered, along with provocations to drive further dialogue on this topic.

title: Access to positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography in the management of lung cancer in Te Manawa Taki Midland Region of New Zealand
abstractText: background: This study examines access to 18-F fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography-computed tomography (FDG PET-CT; PET-CT) scans among lung cancer patients. data and methods: Patients diagnosed with lung cancer in 2011–2021 were identified from the Midland Lung Cancer Register and the New Zealand Cancer Registry. Patients were linked to the National Non-Admitted Patient Collection to determine if they underwent PET-CT. Logistic regression was used to estimate the odds ratios of having PET-CT, adjusting for age, gender, ethnicity, year of diagnosis, socio-economic status, cancer stage, cell type, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) status and comorbidities. results: We identified 613 patients with stage I, 300 with stage II and 3,722 with stages III and IV lung cancer, with 75% of stage I and 68.3% of stage II undergoing PET-CT. PET-CT has become more common over time. Patients aged 80 years and over, Māori, those with frailty (ECOG 2+), and those with stages II–IV of disease were less likely to receive PET-CT. Gender, socio-economic status and comorbidities did not influence the use of PET-CT. conclusion: PET-CT is a standard of care for patients with early-stage lung cancer, suitable for curative treatment. The disparity of access to PET-CT for Māori needs to be addressed.

title: Детекція об'єктів як основа переліку компонентів інтерфейсу для генерації коду зі знімків екрана
abstractText: Під час генерації декларативного коду користувацького інтерфейсу зі знімків екрана мовна модель повинна знати, які саме компоненти присутні на екрані: без цього вона пропускає наявні елементи або додає відсутні. У запропонованій раніше гібридній архітектурі CNN–LLM, де згорткова мережа формує перелік компонентів, а мовна модель генерує за ним код, цей перелік отримували глобальною мультимітковою класифікацією (DenseNet-121 з глобальним усередненням ознак). Такий підхід не дає ні кількості, ні розташування компонентів і погано розпізнає рідкісні віджети. У статті класифікаційне та детекційне формулювання інвентарю порівнюються за однакових умов: обидві моделі використовують 1460 екранів набору Enrico, семантичну розмітку компонентів Rico, однакове розбиття даних і одну метрику якості рівня екрана. Детектор YOLOv8n знаходить компоненти на екрані й обводить їх рамками; клас вважається присутнім з упевненістю, що дорівнює найвищій упевненості серед знайдених рамок цього класу. За правилом рішення, зафіксованим до навчання, і парним бутстрепом детектор підвищує середню точність mAP з 0,566 до 0,659 ± 0,017 за зіставної вхідної роздільності (нижні межі 95 % довірчого інтервалу приросту 0,032–0,067 для трьох запусків) і micro-F1 з 0,706 до 0,806; крім того, він оцінює кількість компонентів точніше за тривіальні базові оцінки для 10 з 14 класів. Приріст не пояснюється розміром об'єктів (ρ Спірмена = −0,09) і є найбільшим для структурних компонентів, тоді як рідкісні віджети обмежені кількістю прикладів і шумом анотацій.

title: Analyse, create, defend: Securing human judgement in marketing communications assessment under generative AI
abstractText: Generative AI has unsettled a long-standing assumption in higher education: that a written submission is evidence of the thinking behind it. This is a particular problem in marketing communications education, where the capabilities that matter most, reading persuasion critically and arguing for a stronger alternative, are those a language model can now imitate. This paper offers a reflective account of an assessment designed in response, currently running in a postgraduate marketing communications subject at an Australian university. Students work in self-selected groups to analyse a real advertisement, then propose and present an improved version as a Pecha Kucha, before defending their decisions in a live discussion with the class and tutor. Generative AI is permitted for producing slide visuals but not for the analysis or argument. The paper argues that a rule of this kind cannot secure an assessment on its own, since compliance cannot be verified, and that what secures the task is the oral defence: a student who has not done the thinking cannot reconstruct it under questioning. This reframing draws on recent work distinguishing discursive from structural assessment change.

title: Designing AI-mediated interactive learning environments for communication skills: Insights from two implementations
abstractText: Developing communication skills remains a core challenge in higher education, particularly in providing scalable opportunities for practice and feedback. This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated systems function as interactive learning environments for communication skills development. Two implementations are examined: a voice-only conversational AI-mediated system used across health disciplines and a digital human avatar used in a business unit. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative survey data and qualitative content. Findings highlighted three key affordances: repeated low-stakes practice, immediate feedback, and flexible engagement. Students reported increased confidence and perceived skill development. Limitations included conversational inaccuracies, realism, technical reliability, and feedback consistency. Importantly, findings indicate that the effectiveness of AI systems is strongly influenced by prompt design, scenario construction, and alignment with learner level. This paper reframes AI tools not as autonomous technologies, but as designed interactive learning environments requiring careful pedagogical integration. Implications are discussed for the design of AI-supported learning activities, particularly in contexts involving oral communication and authentic assessment.

title: The influence of GC-biased gene conversion and recombination rates on the broad-scale patterns of the Pongo genome
abstractText: Abstract The genomic landscape of hominids varies greatly along individual chromosomes, and the role of different population genetic forces - such as mutation, selection, and recombination - in shaping this landscape has been discussed extensively. Here, we apply Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) to orangutan genomes (segmented into 100 kb windows) to identify genomic regions of comparable average G and C base proportion and recombination rate profiles. As expected, inference based on the single and joint allele frequency spectra of the Sumatran and Bornean orangutan species reveals an increasing directional force of biased gene conversion (gBGC) for regions of increasing average GC content. We find these regions to be denser in functional coding regions, with elevated gene expression across multiple tissue types. Regions of different recombination rates differ in their polymorphism, either due to a mutagenic effect of recombination or due to modulation of the effective population size through varying strengths of linked selection, and do not appear directly associated with gBGC. Overall, this indicates that gBGC is a major determinant in the broad-scale background variation, while the effect of recombination beyond the localised impact of recombination hotspots is less clear.

Bridging institutional AI strategy and subject-level teaching practice: A school-level design framework for responsible AI-supported learning
abstractText: The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has accelerated institutional investment in AI infrastructure, yet many universities continue to face difficulties translating institutional strategy into consistent subject-level teaching practice. This paper presents a School-level framework developed at an Australian university. The paper reports the design rationale, outputs and approved deployment model of the framework, including staff capability resources, configurable AI templates, disclosure mechanisms and governance processes. Informed by Educational Design Research and scholarship on organisational change in education, the paper argues that Schools can serve as meso-level environments that enact institutional AI strategy through resources and structures designed to support subject-level teaching practice. It contributes a meso-level governance model, six transferable design principles, and an operational framework intended to support responsible and human-centred AI-supported learning. Formal evaluation is planned following the pilot phase.

title: Be inspired: Connecting educators with authentic teaching practice through Teach HQ
abstractText: Learning and teaching guidance is most effective when it translates principles into practice by showing how educators make design decisions, how students experience those choices, and how others might adapt the approach in their own contexts. This matters in digital learning environments, where educators often need timely, trustworthy and context-sensitive support rather than generic advice. Research on situated learning and communities suggests that professional knowledge develops through participation in shared practice and access to the experiences of more knowledgeable peers (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Wenger, 1998). Similarly, research on professional learning argues that improvement depends not only on exposure to ideas, but also on support for enactment within educators’ own systems of practice (Kennedy, 2016). Reflection and transfer are further strengthened when the context in which practice occurs remains visible (Boud & Walker, 1998).This poster presents Teach HQ, Monash University’s central ecosystem for learning and teaching guidance, as a model for connecting evidence-informed resources with visible, local teaching practice. Teach HQ provides structured guidance across assessment, teaching practices, learning technologies and Moodle. Integrated within the ecosystem, “Be inspired” showcases a collection of concise practice examples from Monash educators. These examples are designed to spark exploration by highlighting real teaching and assessment challenges, the decisions educators made, the resources or technologies used, and practical approaches that others can adopt, adapt and apply.The poster focuses on “Be inspired” as the key motivational entry point into Teach HQ. Rather than presenting guidance as a static repository, “Be inspired” positions educators as active members of a teaching community who learn from authentic examples and lived experiences of their peers. Each story bridges pedagogical guidance and classroom practice by pairing an account of teaching in context with links to additional Teach HQ resources that support adaptation and application. This approach aligns with educational design pattern research, which suggests that teaching knowledge becomes more reusable when successful designs are captured in ways that connect values, context, tasks and resources (Goodyear, 2005).The poster will be structured to allow conference delegates to find their next teaching idea, identify a teaching challenge, explore a “Be inspired” example, and follow linked guidance to plan an adaptation for their own context. It will also share emerging evaluation measures for Teach HQ, including page views, unique visitors, search analytics, stakeholder feedback and growth in “Be inspired” contributions. The intended outcome is for delegates to leave the poster with curiosity, confidence and a practical pathway to explore “Be inspired” and apply at least one new idea in their own teaching.

Reality of Employing Strategic Intelligence in Administrative Decision-Making Process Among Administrative Leaders in Departments of Iraqi Ministry of Youth and Sports: The Employees' Perspective
abstractText: Backgroud: Rebuilding public sports governance and youth empowerment programs in post-conflict Iraq requires adaptive leadership capabilities. This study evaluates the employment of strategic intelligence across its core dimensions (strategic foresight, future vision, strategic knowledge management, and strategic decision-making) among administrative leaders in the Iraqi Ministry of Youth and Sports from the employees' perspective, while determining its predictive contribution to administrative decision-making effectiveness. Methods: A quantitative descriptive-survey and correlational design was conducted across 10 ministry directorates (N = 546). A representative sampling framework engaged 273 personnel, yielding 20 participants for feasibility pre-testing, 100 for psychometric calibration, and 120 for the final empirical investigation. The 24-item validated instrument (6 items per domain on a five-point Likert scale) achieved strong content validity and Cronbach's alpha reliability (0.79). Analytical methods included one-sample t-tests against the theoretical midpoint (18.00), Pearson correlation matrices with 95% confidence intervals, multiple linear regression, and one-way ANOVA across departments. Results: Observed mean scores for all dimensions significantly exceeded the theoretical midpoint benchmark of 18.00 (p < 0.001), with strategic decision-making ranking highest (mean = 19.148, SD = 1.712, t = 7.347) and future vision ranking lowest (mean = 18.664, SD = 1.438, t = 5.056). Bivariate correlation confirmed positive interrelationships connecting foresight, vision, knowledge management, and decision-making (r = 0.528 to 0.615, p < 0.001). Multiple linear regression demonstrated that strategic foresight (beta = 0.357, p < 0.001), knowledge management (beta = 0.312, p < 0.001), and future vision (beta = 0.198, p = 0.012) explained 53.6% of the variance in strategic decision-making (R2 = 0.536, F = 44.62, p < 0.001). One-way ANOVA revealed no significant disparities across the 10 ministry departments (F = 1.054, p = 0.403), indicating a consistent cross-departmental administrative culture. Conclusions: Strategic intelligence serves as a vital driver of administrative agility in post-conflict sports governance. Strengthening institutional foresight mechanisms, modernizing knowledge repositories, and involving personnel in national youth policy formulation provide pragmatic paths to elevating public athletic administration in Iraq.

Clinical profile, quality of life and health needs of Buruli ulcer patients at treatment initiation
abstractText: Abstract Background Little is known about the health needs and quality of life (QoL) of individuals with Buruli ulcer (BU). This study investigated the clinical profile, health needs and QoL of individuals with BU at treatment initiation in Nigeria. Methods This was a descriptive cross-sectional survey of laboratory-confirmed BU patients who are part of the Health needs Assessment for Buruli Ulcer cohort study (HABU-cohort study). A detailed questionnaire was used to obtain the clinical profile of the BU and health needs of the patients. Quality of life was measured using the Cardiff Wound Impact Schedule (CWIS) and the generic EQ-5D-3L QoL tools. Results Of the 60 patients enrolled, 40 (66.7%) were adults (median age 23.50 (10.5, 42.0) years), 31 (51.7%) were female, and 4 (6.7%) of the patients had no formal education. Most of the BU lesions, 48 (80%), occurred within the last five years, and 53 (88.3%) of the patients were presenting with new BU cases. Overall, 41 (68.3%) of the BU lesions were classified as category 3 lesions (> 15 cm), and the median size of the BU was 60.1 (8.7, 133.9) cm². In the CWIS, the physical symptoms and everyday living domain had the lowest mean score of 53.2 (13.1), while the well-being domain had the highest mean score of 81.7 (8.0). In the EQ-5D-3L tools, more than half of the patients reported having some problems in their mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression domains. Overall, the QoL scores of the patients showed no statistically significant differences according to their socio-demographic and clinical characteristics ( p > 0.05). In addition, we found that BU patients tend to have substantial health care, economic, and social needs, but less so for environmental needs. Conclusions BU substantially affects the physical symptoms, everyday living, and social life domains of QoL, irrespective of the demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients. This is accompanied by substantial health care, economic, and social needs. An integrated and decentralized skin health strategy may be utilized to address these needs and improve the QoL of BU patients.

title: When curators become creators: A community of practice approach to vibe coding for teacher designers
abstractText: This study examines how participation in a community of practice (CoP) supports primary school educators in becoming designers of teaching and learning through vibe coding. Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework of teaching as design science, end-user development, and CoP theory, this qualitative case study traces the journeys of the Visionary Learning Collective (VLC), a community that began with five primary school teachers in South Korea with little to no prior knowledge of computer science. Analysis of focus group interviews, observational data, and participant artefacts revealed three themes: growth as a designer, growth as a developer, and growth through community. Findings suggest that vibe coding may have functioned as a threshold-like experience that reorients teacher identity from curator to creator, that the CoP provided the affective infrastructure necessary for this transition, and that participation generated cascading circles of legitimate peripheral participation extending beyond the original community.

title: Code-Switching and Code-Mixing in Classroom Interaction in Class IX.2 of SMP Negeri 15 Padang
abstractText: Although code-switching and code-mixing are widely studied in sociolinguistics, their use in Indonesian language lessons involving Indonesian and Minangkabau remains insufficiently described at the junior high school level. This study examined their forms, frequencies, and patterns in classroom interactions in Class IX.2 at SMP Negeri 15 Padang. A quantitative descriptive design was employed. Data were collected through classroom observations and recordings of teacher–student interactions. Recorded utterances were transcribed, identified, classified, and analyzed using frequencies and percentages. The analysis identified 40 linguistic events, comprising 15 instances of code-switching (37.5%) and 25 instances of code-mixing (62.5%). Among code-switching events, 9 involved shifts from Indonesian to Minangkabau (60%), while 6 involved the reverse direction (40%). Code-mixing comprised word insertion (17 instances; 68%), phrase insertion (6 instances; 24%), and clause insertion (2 instances; 8%). Teachers produced 25 events (62.5%), while students produced 15 (37.5%). Code-mixing was therefore more frequent than code-switching, with word insertion constituting its most common form. These findings provide a descriptive account of bilingual language use in the observed classroom and contribute contextual evidence to sociolinguistic research on Indonesian language learning. The study highlights the importance of teachers’ awareness of language choices to support classroom communication while maintaining Indonesian as the language of instruction.

title: Artefact or evidence? Clarifying what counts in programmatic learning portfolios
abstractText: Australian higher education is moving toward programmatic assessment, a shift given further impetus by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency’s (TEQSA) 2023 discussion paper on assessment reform in the age of artificial intelligence. This calls for a systemic approach to program assessment aligned with disciplines and qualifications, rather than one confined to individual units (Lodge et al., 2023). Within this shift, the digital portfolio has become a mechanism for evidencing achievement across whole degree programs. Portfolios in this context typically hold a growing accumulation of materials such as assignments, placement records, project outputs, and reflective writing. As students collect artefacts across a program, the portfolio becomes a means of making their learning visible over time, reframing assessment as an ongoing process of meaning making rather than a series of isolated judgements (Baartman & Quinlan, 2023). This poster argues that the value of a portfolio depends less on the volume of material it holds than on a distinction that is often assumed rather than made explicit: the difference between an artefact and evidence. An artefact is any product or record of student activity: an assignment, presentation, a reflection. It becomes evidence only once interpreted against a stated outcome or standard, connecting the artefact to the claim is meant to support (Baartman & Quinlan, 2023). Without this connection, a portfolio functions as a repository of activity rather than a demonstration of learning. This distinction carries weight in programmatic assessment, where judgement is distributed rather than concentrated in a single task, and students and academic staff track development across a program of study. A set of specified standards is defined for each level of the program, which students must attain by the end of each phase. High-stakes decisions at these milestones are made by a panel weighing multiple, longitudinal artefacts against a program’s stated outcomes. This shift improves the defensibility and transparency of judgement while making learning visible over time (Baartman et al., 2022). Treated simply as collection points, portfolios risk becoming unwieldy and meaningless. When the artefact-evidence distinction is built into portfolio design, teaching and staff development from the outset, it offers a mechanism for students and programs to make cumulative, defensible claims about learning and graduate capabilities. This poster presents a framework distinguishing artefact from evidence, developed through curriculum transformation work at an Australian university moving toward programmatic learning. It sets out three conditions under which an artefact functions as evidence: alignment to a named outcome or standard, an explicit reflective or interpretive act connecting the artefact to that outcome, and a level of specificity that allows a marker or reviewer to assess the claim rather than merely acknowledge the artefact’s existence. The framework is intended as a practical reference point for curriculum designers, staff, and students working with portfolios in programmatic contexts. Delegates are invited to discuss how this distinction might apply, in their own programmatic curriculum work, where it breaks down in practice, and what it asks of the human relationship between student and assessor.

title: From tools to sense-making: Designing a human-centred AI workshop
abstractText: Generative AI raises identity- and values-level questions for higher education staff. Yet professional development in this space remains largely focused on individualised technical and pedagogical skill and capability development, rather than providing structured opportunities for the collective sense-making such questions require. This paper describes the design and delivery of a human-centred workshop developed for a team of higher education third space practitioners to support collective sense-making and values negotiation around AI use. Drawing on reflective practitioner inquiry, we describe the design principles that shaped the workshop and the practical constraints within which it was delivered. We reflect on what worked, including the value of structured formats in supporting deeper engagement, and of workshop artefacts as an evolving record of shared thinking. We suggest this design offers a transferable approach for other educator teams grappling with similar uncertainty, and propose that professional development for AI should complement skills-focused approaches with structured space for the collective exploration of values, judgement, and human agency.

Designing assessment through transformation: A learning beyond the classroom approach to AI-mediated assessment
abstractText: Where does meaningful learning begin in an era of generative artificial intelligence (AI)? Current responses to AI in higher education have largely focused on assessment redesign, academic integrity and AI literacy. While these developments have strengthened assessment practice, they often assume that meaningful learning begins when students enter university. This paper argues that responding effectively to AI requires reconsidering this assumption. Drawing upon the learning beyond the classroom framework, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy for assessment design that recognises learners’ existing educational resources and supports their development into disciplinary judgement. This paper contributes in three ways. First, it introduces the learning beyond the classroom framework as a conceptual foundation for understanding learning in AI-mediated higher education. Second, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy that connects recognition, translation, transformation and disciplinary judgement within a developmental approach to assessment design. Third, it translates this philosophy into five practical principles that provide educators with a flexible lens for redesigning assessment across diverse disciplinary contexts. Rather than treating AI as the central educational challenge, the paper positions it as a catalyst for reconsidering the purposes of assessment, arguing that higher education’s enduring contribution lies in cultivating critical judgement, ethical reasoning and meaningful contribution.

From doing the work to shaping the work: Reflections from an ASCILITE community mentoring journey on leadership and influence
abstractText: The pressing pace of change in higher education has created a greater demand for professionals who can influence practice, spearhead innovation and navigate complexity beyond the confines of their formal roles. Although mentoring is widely recognised as a valuable form of professional development (Zachary, 2012), community-based mentoring models that combine individual development with collective reflection and shared learning have received less attention. This poster reflects on a six-month journey undertaken through the ASCILITE Community Mentoring Program, involving three mentees and two mentors from different institutions and professional contexts. Each participant entered the program with different goals that included leading organisational change, advancing curriculum and assessment innovation, and strengthening leadership presence and communication. Yet the group shared a common aspiration: to strengthen their capability to influence practice, people and institutional direction, moving beyond technical expertise. Drawing on mentoring conversations, reflective activities, peer discussion and individual project work, the poster presents each participant’s personal development story alongside a synthesis of the common themes identified through iterative reflection and discussion. The reflective approach provided insights into how these professionals experienced professional growth through structured reflection, dialogue, challenge and sense-making within a supportive community, rather than through the acquisition of new knowledge (Lave & Wenger, 1991; Schön, 1983; Wenger, 1998). A key outcome of the program is the proposed development of a simple working model of professional influence (Doing – Understanding – Leading – Shaping). This model will surface how experience can be transformed through reflection and conversation into insight, leading to action and ultimately greater influence within professional contexts. Across the three journeys, participants were prompted to consider their shift in thinking from doing to understanding, from understanding to leading, and from leading to shaping practice and change. This poster argues that community mentoring can provide more than just career guidance and motivation. It creates a space for professional identity formation, critical reflection, and the development of leadership capability by facilitating connections with others who are facing similar challenges. In a complex and continually changing sector, these reflections highlight the importance of conversation, community and reflective practice as the basis for professional growth and influence.

The apprenticeship layer: What assessment reform cannot secure on its own
abstractText: Australian higher education has responded to generative artificial intelligence with an ambitious program of assessment reform. Structural approaches, most visibly the two-lane model, seek to sustain trust in degrees by securing some assessments while opening others to AI partnership. This conceptual paper argues that the reform consensus, now sharpened by sector attention to assurance of learning and adaptive capabilities, addresses validity more directly than formation. Assessment tasks are not only measurement occasions; they can also be sites of the cognitive work through which capability develops. Drawing on cognitive apprenticeship, desirable difficulties and cognitive offloading, the paper introduces the apprenticeship layer: the stratum of entry-level cognitive work through which expertise has historically been developed and renewed. As AI is increasingly used to perform parts of this work in workplaces and universities, institutions face a risk of certifying capabilities without reliably preserving the practice through which those capabilities are formed. The paper proposes three principles for formation-centred design: friction by design, process as both learning and evidence, and a care floor of guaranteed human attention. It concludes that valid judgement and capability formation are different questions that assessment can and should be designed to answer together.

Dari Akhlak ke Karakter: Sintesis Pemikiran Al-Ghazali, Ahmad Dahlan, dan Thomas Lickona
abstractText: Pendidikan karakter dalam konteks pendidikan kontemporer membutuhkan landasan moral yang tidak hanya menekankan pengetahuan mengenai nilai, tetapi juga proses internalisasi dan aktualisasi nilai dalam kehidupan. Dalam pendidikan Islam, konsep akhlak memiliki fondasi spiritual yang kuat, sedangkan teori pendidikan karakter modern memberikan penjelasan mengenai proses pembentukan moral secara kognitif, afektif, dan perilaku. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis konstruksi pendidikan karakter dalam pemikiran Al-Ghazali, K.H. Ahmad Dahlan, dan Thomas Lickona serta mensintesiskan ketiga pemikiran tersebut menjadi kerangka pendidikan karakter Islam yang relevan bagi pendidikan kontemporer. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan metode library research. Data diperoleh melalui penelusuran dan analisis literatur yang relevan mengenai pemikiran ketiga tokoh, pendidikan akhlak, dan pendidikan karakter. Data dianalisis secara tematik-komparatif melalui tiga dimensi, yaitu landasan, tujuan, dan proses pembentukan karakter. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa Al-Ghazali menempatkan akhlak dan pembinaan jiwa sebagai fondasi moral, K.H. Ahmad Dahlan menghubungkan nilai keagamaan dengan pengamalan sosial, sedangkan Thomas Lickona menjelaskan pembentukan karakter melalui moral knowing, moral feeling, dan moral action. Sintesis ketiga pemikiran menghasilkan kerangka konseptual nilai → kesadaran → pembiasaan → tindakan moral, dengan Al-Ghazali memberikan fondasi spiritual-akhlak, Ahmad Dahlan memberikan orientasi sosial-praksis, dan Lickona memberikan struktur psikopedagogis pembentukan karakter. Penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa akhlak dan karakter dapat didialogkan secara komplementer untuk membangun pendidikan karakter Islam yang integratif, dengan tetap mempertahankan kekhasan fondasi moral Islam dan relevansinya terhadap kebutuhan pendidikan kontemporer

Lecturer–Student Bullying and the Paradox of Belonging in Two Ghanaian Public Universities
abstractText: Lecturer–student bullying has been linked to adverse academic and psychological outcomes but, little is known about how forms of bullying affect students' sense of belonging in higher education. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined this relationship in two Ghanaian universities. Quantitative data from 642 undergraduates were analysed using multiple linear regression, and qualitative data from 16 selected participants using reflexive thematic analysis to explain findings. Cyberbullying significantly predicted lower levels of belonging, whereas physical, verbal, and relational bullying were not significant predictors. The regression model explained 18.5% of the variance in students' sense of belonging. Contrary to expectations, sexual bullying was positively associated with belonging. The qualitative findings helped explain this paradox by showing that some students perceived lecturer attention associated with sexual bullying as conferring academic advantages, preferential treatment, or social recognition. These perceived benefits appeared to shape students' experiences of belonging despite the exploitative nature of the relationships. Lecturer–student bullying influences students' sense of belonging in complex and sometimes contradictory ways. The findings suggest that belonging within hierarchical educational contexts may not always reflect genuine inclusion but may instead be shaped by unequal power relations and perceived benefits. Universities should strengthen institutional policies, reporting mechanisms, and professional standards to prevent lecturer bullying while fostering safe and authentic forms of student belonging.

Making programming learning visible: Students’ perceptions of an authentic, process-oriented assessment design
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased questions about whether a final code artefact alone can constitute sufficient evidence of student learning in programming education. This poster presents a practice-based evaluation of a redesigned second-year programming unit that incorporated multiple forms of evidence of learning. The assessment design is informed by authentic assessment (Boud & Molloy, 2013), feedback for learning (Carless & Boud, 2018) and self-explanation theory (Chi et al., 1989). It responded to current calls for assessment reform in the age of AI by shifting attention from the final artefact to the processes through which students design, explain, test and improve code (Lodge et al., 2023). Across three progressively sequenced assessments, students produced working Python programs, submitted WakaTime development records, recorded video explanations of design decisions, declared and justified GenAI use where permitted, and revisited prior code to improve exception handling and pytest testing. GenAI was allowed under accountable-use conditions, during which students were required to identify GenAI-assisted code, ensure that their submissions used concepts taught in the unit, and demonstrate that they understood and could explain the code they submitted. Assessment 1 established foundational object-oriented programming practices. Assessment 2 asked students to build a weather-data bot using CSV data, web scraping, datetime, logging, collections and pandas analysis. Assessment 3 required students to return to their Assessment 2 codebase and use feedback from Assessment 2 to strengthen its robustness through built-in exceptions, custom exceptions and tests. The design operationalised process-oriented assessment at task level. Code provided product evidence; WakaTime provided process evidence; video explanation provided conceptual evidence; and feedback with staged task design supported iterative development. Together, these tasks created an evidentiary architecture that made programming processes, conceptual reasoning and judgement more visible than final code alone. The evaluation drew on 68 anonymous unit feedback responses. Open-ended feedback was examined using thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017). Three student-perception themes were emergent. First, authentic tasks positioned programming as professional practice: students valued project-based tasks such as CSV analysis, web scraping and data-processing bots because they resembled meaningful programming work. Second, explanation and process evidence made computational thinking visible: students described shifts from writing code to thinking in terms of modularity, validation, debugging and engineering practice. Third, feedback supported iterative improvement and confidence: students reported that feedback helped them identify errors, revise code and progress more independently. The poster argues that process-oriented programming assessment should not rely only on restricting AI use. Instead, assessment can require multiple forms of evidence to validate student learning (Dawson et al., 2024) such as working code, development traces, self-explanatory video, feedback uptake, accountable AI-use declarations and testing artefacts. Video explanation is especially important because it prompts students to justify programing structures, methods, strategies and data-analysis approaches (Lai & Niblock, 2024). The study is limited by its reliance on one unit, one teaching period and self-reported student feedback. Further analysis of WakaTime data, video explanations, code revisions and pytest artefacts will examine how process evidence relates to conceptual understanding, reasoning and feedback uptake.

Beyond conversation length: Conversation openings, cognitive engagement, and support orientations in student-AI chatbot interactions
abstractText: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

Teaching beyond AI: Gamified problem-based formative assessment aligned with UNESCO AI competency frameworks
abstractText: The arrival of capable generative AI (GenAI) tools has posed a genuine and largely unresolved challenge for summative assessment in higher education. When AI-generated submissions evade institutional detection 94% of the time and examination scores rise sharply without any change in teaching, the evidentiary basis of take-home and invigilated assessment is genuinely in question. This paper draws on two lines of work to argue that classroom-based gamified problem-based formative assessment (GPBFA) offers a more durable response than detection-focused approaches. The first line is an empirical study of saval.app, a GPBFA platform evaluated through Keller’s ARCS motivational model across a full university semester (pre n = 41, post n = 44). Results across all four ARCS dimensions were encouraging (all p < .0001; Cronbach’s alpha > .93; composite 81% positive response rate), with near-zero motivational decline across 12 weeks. The second line is a review of UNESCO’s 2024 AI Competency Frameworks for Teachers and Students, which we argue are philosophically and pedagogically aligned with classroom GPBFA in ways the existing literature has not yet made explicit. Taken together, we suggest that moving assessment into the classroom — where it is live, observed, and problem-centred — may address both the integrity challenge and the AI literacy imperative that UNESCO frameworks define.

title: A case study of wellbeing-centred learning design in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs)
abstractText: As higher education increasingly embraces fully online and scalable learning environments, concerns regarding digital fatigue, distraction, social isolation, disengagement, and learner wellbeing have become more prominent. Recent studies suggest that online learning environments are most effective when they support not only cognitive outcomes but also emotional, social, and motivational needs. This paper presents a case study of the redesign of UNSW Canberra’s two massive open online courses (MOOCs). Using compassion as a guiding design lens, the case demonstrates how emerging Coursera capabilities, such as AI-supported dialogue items, role play activities, authentic assessments, and facilitated discussion opportunities, were intentionally implemented to address known challenges in online learning. The paper also analyses how this design intervention was intentionally aligned with wellbeing-centred learning design principles. Preliminary course analytics following redesign provide encouraging indicators, including increased learner engagement and improved completion rates across both MOOCs. While these outcomes do not establish causal relationships between individual interventions and learner behaviour, they suggest that wellbeing-centred learning design may positively contribute to learner participation and persistence in large-scale online learning environments. The study highlights the potential of compassion as a practical design lens for creating more supportive, inclusive, and learner-centred digital learning experiences.

Conversational pedagogy in practice: Exploring a unit-embedded GenAI chatbot in higher education
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are increasingly being adopted in higher education; however, limited research has examined their pedagogical integration within learning environments. This paper reports findings from an exploratory mixed-methods case study of a GenAI chatbot embedded in a postgraduate unit at an Australian university. Designed as a pedagogically embedded learning companion, the chatbot provided contextualised guidance and functioned as a first point of contact for students seeking clarification and support. Findings indicate that students perceived the chatbot as a useful and accessible learning resource that supported engagement, reflection, and self-directed learning. Three themes emerged: first-contact pedagogical support, AI-mediated scaffolding, and human-AI complementarity. Students valued the immediacy and contextual relevance of responses while recognising the continuing importance of educator guidance. These initial findings provide insights into the design of pedagogically embedded GenAI learning companions and their potential role in supporting learning within higher education.

title: Violence and Trauma in Two African Women’s Autobiographies
abstractText: This study examines representations of trauma, violence, and resilience in two African women’s autobiographies: A Toast to Life (2018) by Ghanaian actress and philanthropist Juliet Ibrahim and Brutal Legacy (2019) by South African broadcaster Tracy Going. Using a qualitative narrative case study design informed by Judith Herman’s trauma theory and a transcultural perspective, the study explores how the authors construct and make meaning of traumatic experiences across different socio-cultural contexts. Thematic analysis revealed three interconnected themes: trauma as a lifelong and multidimensional experience; violence as both a personal experience and a social reality; and the intergenerational and cultural transmission of trauma. The findings show that trauma is cumulative and enduring, manifesting through childhood abuse, war-related displacement, intimate partner violence, grief, and psychological distress. Violence is represented not only as physical harm but also as emotional, psychological, cultural, and structural oppression sustained by patriarchal norms, silence, and institutional failures. The narratives further reveal how trauma is transmitted across generations through family histories, collective memories, and cultural expectations. Despite these experiences, both autobiographies foreground resilience, recovery, and identity reconstruction through storytelling. The findings imply that African women’s autobiographical writing functions as a powerful form of testimony, resistance, and healing that transforms private suffering into collective awareness while challenging gendered systems of oppression and silencing.

title: Field necropsy findings in removed sows from a spanish breeding system: primary causes of removal and concomitant lesions
abstractText: Abstract Background This study investigated the probable causes of removal over a one-year period in a Spanish breeding herd, as well as the frequency and patterns of concomitant macroscopic findings. Sow mortality and involuntary removal remain major welfare and economic concerns in modern pig production, with rising rates reported internationally. Field necropsy, although not a substitute for complementary laboratory diagnostics, is a practical tool to establish the probable cause of removal. However, causes of removal are typically reported and interpreted individually, with limited attention to whether concomitant findings relate to the primary problem or to a sow’s ultimate failure to recover. Results Field necropsies were performed on 319 removed sows in a production system of approximately 10 000 sows in south-eastern Spain, November 2024-August 2025, of which 178 (55.8%) were euthanized and 141 (44.2%) died spontaneously. Locomotor disorders were the leading cause (86/319, 27.0%), followed by visceral torsion (46, 14.4%), prolapse (46, 14.4%; uterine, rectal, or bladder), and undetermined causes (40, 12.5%). A concomitant macroscopic finding, distinct from the stated primary cause, was recorded in 236/319 sows (74.0%), and two or more concomitant findings co-occurred in 116/319 (36.4%). The most frequent concomitant findings were macroscopic bladder lesions (68/319, 21.3%), digestive/gastrointestinal findings (64/319, 20.1%) and pulmonary lesions (55/319, 17.2%). Among sows removed for poor body condition/cachexia (20/319, 6.3%), a concomitant finding was present in 15/20 (75.0%), most often a locomotor lesion (9/20, 45.0%); a documented prior treatment attempt was recorded in 6/20 (30.0%), all of which ultimately failed to recover. Conclusions Concomitant macroscopic findings were common and frequently co-occurred with the stated primary cause of removal, rather than presenting as isolated findings. Systematic field necropsy, beyond establishing a single probable cause, may help identify sows in which multiple, possibly interrelated, processes — including subclinical pathology not apparent in life — could be compromising health, welfare and the likelihood of recovery.

What makes AI educational? A sociocultural framework for transforming AI from artefact to mediating tool
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet much of its use positions AI as a private productivity tool for generating answers, feedback or text. This paper argues that AI is not educational simply because it produces outputs. From a sociocultural perspective, its educational significance emerges when pedagogical design transforms it from an artefact into a mediating tool for participation in disciplinary learning. The paper introduces the AI Mediated Participation Framework, grounded in mediated learning, appropriation and participation. It proposes three design principles: preserving learner ownership, scaffolding thinking through dialogue, and developing AI literacy through disciplinary practice. These principles operate through questioning, dialogue, reflection, critical evaluation and decision making to support learner agency, evaluative judgement, responsible AI use, critical thinking and knowledge construction. The framework is illustrated through AI learning activities in undergraduate and postgraduate educational research courses, where educator modelling, peer discussion and disciplinary expectations repositioned AI from a private feedback service to a mediating tool for methodological reasoning and researcher judgement. The framework shifts attention from what AI can do to how pedagogical design determines what AI becomes educationally.

title: Strategi Pengelolaan Keuangan dalam Mendukung Profitabilitas dan Keberlanjutan Perusahaan: Tinjauan Literatur
abstractText: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengidentifikasi dan menganalisis strategi pengelolaan keuangan dalam mendukung peningkatan profitabilitas dan keberlanjutan perusahaan berdasarkan hasil penelitian terdahulu. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan metode literature review melalui tahapan perencanaan, pelaksanaan kajian, dan pelaporan. Literatur yang relevan dianalisis dengan membandingkan hasil penelitian serta mengelompokkannya ke dalam beberapa tema, yaitu pengelolaan modal kerja dan arus kas, pengendalian biaya dan efisiensi operasional, keputusan investasi dan pendanaan, perencanaan dan evaluasi kinerja keuangan, serta hubungan strategi pengelolaan keuangan dengan keberlanjutan perusahaan. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa pengelolaan modal kerja dan arus kas berperan dalam menjaga kelancaran operasional, pengendalian biaya mendukung efisiensi penggunaan sumber daya, sedangkan keputusan investasi dan pendanaan membantu perusahaan mengalokasikan dana dengan mempertimbangkan manfaat serta risiko keuangan. Selain itu, perencanaan dan evaluasi kinerja keuangan diperlukan untuk memastikan bahwa keputusan yang diambil sesuai dengan kondisi dan tujuan perusahaan. Kajian ini juga menunjukkan bahwa profitabilitas yang tinggi tidak selalu mencerminkan keberlanjutan usaha apabila tidak disertai pengelolaan likuiditas, risiko, struktur utang, dan tata kelola yang baik. Dengan demikian, strategi pengelolaan keuangan perlu diterapkan secara menyeluruh dan disesuaikan dengan karakteristik perusahaan agar pencapaian keuntungan dapat berjalan seimbang dengan kemampuan mempertahankan usaha dalam jangka panjang.

title: Health Screening, Education, and Physical Activity Program for Older Adults in Mulyorejo Urban Village
abstractText: Hypertension and diabetes mellitus are important noncommunicable disease concerns among older adults. In RW 07, Mulyorejo Urban Village, initial screening identified elevated blood pressure and random blood glucose findings among participating older adults. Aim: This community service activity aimed to provide early health screening, health education, and physical activity promotion for older adults. Methods: The activity was conducted in RW 07, Mulyorejo Urban Village, Sukun District, Malang City, from 18 to 26 July 2026. Forty older adults participated in the screening and the SEHATI and LENTERA activities. Data were obtained from a screening record sheet containing blood pressure and random blood glucose results and from direct observation of program implementation. No validated pre–post knowledge questionnaire or post-intervention blood pressure/glucose assessment was documented; therefore, changes in knowledge or clinical measurements were not evaluated. Results: Initial screening found 27 of 40 participants (67.5%) with blood pressure categorized as high in the activity record and 15 of 40 participants (37.5%) with random blood glucose (RBG) above 110 mg/dL. The available records do not provide participant-level demographic characteristics or post-intervention measurements. Conclusion: The activities enabled initial identification of blood pressure and glucose findings that require appropriate follow-up. The results should be interpreted as descriptive screening findings and implementation of health promotion activities, not evidence of improved knowledge or reduced blood pressure/glucose levels.

Computational and experimental strategies for functional validation of non-coding variants in pancreatic cancer
abstractText: Abstract Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterised by extensive genomic heterogeneity and limited therapeutic options. Although recurrent coding mutations in key driver genes have been well researched, large-scale sequencing studies have identified a broad array of non-coding variants which may contribute to tumorigenesis by interfering with gene regulatory mechanisms. However, understanding the functional significance of these variants remains a major challenge due to their abundance and the complexity of non-coding regulatory structures. This review outlines current computational and experimental techniques to identify, prioritise, and functionally validate non-coding variants in PDAC. We discuss in silico methods including genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapping, colocalisation, machine learning-driven functional annotation, and the use of established computational tools, in addition to epigenomic profiling technologies including, ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and CUT&RUN which define regulatory landscapes. We also emphasise new AI-based methods involving radiogenomics, AI imaging analysis and data integration, which provides novel potential to link genomic variation with phenotypic and imaging characteristics. Additionally, we highlight experimental validation techniques including reporter assays, electrophoretic mobility shift assays (EMSA), chromatin conformation capture methods, and CRISPR-based perturbation systems used to study variant functionality. Together, these complementary approaches establish a framework for correlating non-coding variation to regulatory mechanisms in PDAC.

Designing human-AI creative learning: A scoping review towards a human-centred framework for AI-assisted creativity in higher education
abstractText: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education by reshaping how learners generate ideas, solve problems, and engage in creative knowledge construction. While existing research has primarily examined the effectiveness of AI tools on learning outcomes, writing performance, and student engagement, comparatively little attention has been paid to understanding how educators intentionally design AI-assisted creative learning experiences. This paper presents a scoping review of 49 empirical and conceptual sources on AI-assisted creativity in higher education to identify recurring instructional design practices, human–AI interaction patterns, and pedagogical strategies. Rather than focusing on technological capabilities alone, the review synthesizes how creative learning activities are structured around collaboration between learners, educators, and AI systems, while also engaging directly with mixed evidence on AI’s creative value, including findings that AI-assisted ideation can expand idea novelty under some conditions, yet produce design fixation and narrowed divergent thinking under others. Building upon this synthesis, the paper proposes a preliminary Human-Centered AI Creativity Design (HACD) framework that positions AI as a collaborative creative partner while preserving learner agency, critical reflection, and ethical decision-making. The framework offers an initial conceptual model to guide educators in designing meaningful AI-supported creative learning experiences and provides a foundation for empirical validation.

When AI talks back: A cross-disciplinary study of educator design judgment in AI-assisted case development
abstractText: Educators are increasingly turning to generative AI when developing teaching materials, yet most research to date has centred on student-facing applications. This paper presents a work-in-progress study that asks a different question: what happens to an educator’s design judgment when AI enters the case-writing process? Two business educators – one in accounting, one in management – will each develop a teaching case study using AI-assisted workflows, documenting their prompts, editorial decisions, and reasoning through structured process logs. Drawing on Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner framework and Abell’s (1997) 10 criteria for effective teaching cases, the study examines where human expertise proves essential and where AI contributes meaningfully. The pairing of two sub-disciplines, management accounting and management, allows us to examine whether disciplinary knowledge shapes these design decisions in distinct ways, although the study’s central concern remain the design judgement itself. Early observations from the instrument development phase point to a useful distinction: AI appears better suited to qualities that require evaluative judgment (structure, data accuracy, length) than those demanding generative judgment (ambiguity, controversy, authentic voice). We expect further patterns to emerge once data collection begins. This paper outlines the research design and its anticipated contributions.

title: Teacher–GenAI partnership in design and technology education: From utility to allyship
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping Design and Technology (D&T) education by transforming how design ideas are generated, evaluated, and refined. Although existing research has largely focused on capabilities and limitations of AI, less is known about the emerging teacher–GenAI relationships during authentic design practice. Through semi-structured and recall interviews, classroom observations, reflective journals, design folios and artefacts, this qualitative case study investigated these relationships. Guided by sociomaterial perspectives and using reflexive thematic analysis, the study examined how creativity, agency, knowledge construction, pedagogy, and ethical decision-making emerged through human–GenAI interaction. Findings revealed that pre-service teacher–GenAI partnerships evolved through a developmental trajectory from utility, to dialogue, to teacher orchestration, and ultimately allyship. Rather than functioning as a solution-generating tool, GenAI became a provocateur and generative partner whose educational value emerged through iterative cycles of prompting, critique, reflection, and redesign. The study proposes Orchestrated Co-Agency and the Teacher–GenAI Relationship Continuum as complementary conceptual lenses for understanding these interactions. These lenses could offer new theoretical insights into human–AI co-creation and inform curriculum, pedagogy, and the responsible integration of GenAI in Design and Technology education.

Long-term survival after sleeve lobectomy versus pneumonectomy for non-small cell lung cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstractText: Abstract Background Sleeve lobectomy (SL) preserves lung parenchyma in selected patients with centrally located non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We updated the comparative evidence on SL versus pneumonectomy (PN), focusing on long-term survival and perioperative outcomes. Methods PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched to June 10, 2025, for studies comparing SL with PN. Individual observations were reconstructed from published Kaplan–Meier curves with study identifiers retained. Study-specific hazard ratios (HRs) were pooled using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) with modified Hartung–Knapp confidence intervals, and a study-stratified Cox model was fitted as a complementary analysis. Perioperative outcomes were pooled with the same random-effects approach. Results Twenty-seven studies were included, of which 25 contributed to the meta-analysis. SL was associated with better overall survival (OS; 19 studies, 5,491 patients; HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.55–0.70) and disease-free survival (DFS; seven studies, 3,675 patients; HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.61–0.81), and with lower 30-day (OR 0.54, 95% CI 0.31–0.92) and 90-day mortality (OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.17–0.77). Bronchopleural fistula, reoperation, and hospital stay did not differ significantly. The OS association persisted among matched cohorts (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.52–0.75), whereas pooled source-reported multivariable estimates were less precise (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.48–1.03). Conclusions In observational cohorts, SL was associated with better long-term survival and lower early mortality than PN. Residual confounding by indication precludes causal inference, but the findings support parenchyma-preserving sleeve resection when an R0 resection is technically and oncologically feasible.

title: Cynical views as barriers for change: Legal attitudes and willingness to change among formerly incarcerated individuals
Closing the loop by design: A process and system for turning unit reflection into tracked action
abstractText: Teaching teams in higher education are asked to reflect on teaching delivery and propose improvements for future periods, yet insights often remain at the level of reflection and rarely lead to tracked follow-up. Proposed actions are recorded but not systematically closed, leaving the quality-improvement loop incomplete. This paper reports the design of a unit action plan process and supporting system intended to close that loop. The process combines a single reflective template, status-tracked action items, and discipline-based review meetings that function as communities of practice. Educational designers participate to support pedagogical decisions while the system makes collaboration and follow-up visible. Synthesis of themes across action plans provides a faculty-wide view of teaching quality, with analytics supporting decision-making. We describe the workflow from reflection to tracked action and report early outcomes from faculty-wide use. We argue that closing the loop is a design problem of workflow, ownership, and educational technology, and we offer principles other institutions can adapt.

title: Beyond sacral slope change: a new lumbar flexion-based hip-spine classification for total hip arthroplasty
abstractText: Aims The complex interplay between spinopelvic alignment and total hip arthroplasty (THA) outcomes has led to classification systems guiding acetabular component positioning. However, current systems rely heavily on sacral slope change (ΔSS) as a proxy for spinal mobility, despite emerging evidence questioning its accuracy. We introduce the Lumbar-Flexion Hip-Spine (LF-HS) classification (LF system), a novel system prioritizing true lumbar flexion (LF ≤ 20°) over ΔSS to assess spinal stiffness. This study compares the LF system with the established sacral-slope-based classification and evaluates its use in risk stratification and surgical planning. Methods In a retrospective cohort of 1,795 primary THA cases in 1,673 patients (mean age 66.1 years (23 to 94)), preoperative spinopelvic radiographs were analyzed to determine pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis (PI-LL) mismatch, ΔSS, LF, and pelvic mobility parameters, including standing pelvic tilt (PT) and change in PT from flexed seated to standing (ΔPT). These were used as modifiers in the LF system. Patients were classified using both systems. We assessed group distributions, prevalence of spinopelvic risk factors, Hip User Index (HUI), and dislocation rates. Statistical comparisons included McNemar’s test and linear regression. Results The LF system identified 4% (n = 72) of patients as having spinal stiffness (LF ≤ 20°) compared with 41.9% (n = 753) using the SS system (ΔSS < 10%) (p < 0.001). LF-defined stiff spine groups showed significantly higher HUI scores ≥ 80%, indicating greater hip-dependent motion and dislocation risk. The two-year dislocation rate was 0.6%, lower than national benchmarks. The LF system demonstrated better age correlation and risk discrimination than the SS system. Conclusion The LF classification offers a more precise, mobility-driven approach to spinopelvic assessment in THA. Incorporating functional pelvic modifiers and replacing ΔSS with LF improves preoperative planning and may reduce complications, particularly dislocation. Adoption of the LF system may refine surgical decision-making towards a more individualized, biomechanics-based approach. Cite this article: Bone Jt Open 2026;7(11):1489–1497.
