Mentoring for renewal: Moving beyond professional development
abstractText: This reflective narrative reframes mentoring beyond its conventional role as a vehicle for career advancement and professional development. Drawing on two years of participation in the Women in Academic Leadership (WiAL) Program, this autoethnographic account explores how mentoring functions as a space for nurturing ideas, identifying opportunities, and sustaining personal growth. In this context, the mentoring relationship is conceptualised as a socially mediated site of learning that enabled processes of social integration, meaning-making, and sharing of cultural understanding and wisdom. Through our shared experience as late mid-career to senior academic women, we argue that the most transformative dimensions of mentoring are often its least visible: the quiet expansion of possibility, the lighting of alternative pathways, and the relational holding of potential. We offer this account as a contribution to conversations about reflective practice and career communities in higher education, particularly for those navigating institutions where traditional markers of progression are opaque, political, or structurally limited.

title: An assistive Braille proofreading system for empowering lay volunteers
abstractText: Braille literature serves as a critical conduit for individuals with visual impairments to access information, deepen learning, and achieve professional self-actualization (Ryles, 1996). However, transcribing Chinese texts into Taiwanese Braille poses unique and formidable challenges. Unlike alphabetic languages, Chinese is a logographic language consisting of thousands of distinct characters. Crucially, Taiwanese Braille does not directly map onto Chinese characters but is instead intrinsically bound to their phonetic values via the Zhuyin system (Hung, 2008). Consequently, a single character can carry entirely different pronunciations and Braille representations depending on its semantic context, rendering polyphonic characters the primary bottleneck in automated transcription. Beyond Taiwanese Braille, Japanese Braille confronts analogous hurdles in homonym confusion (Seto et al., 2023)—the inverse of the polyphonic challenge—reflecting a persistent dilemma across character-based Asian orthographies. To correct errors induced by polyphonic ambiguities, Braille literature must undergo rigorous proofreading prior to publication. Traditional proofreading relies heavily on cumbersome manual workflows, typically executed via two approaches: a collaborative dyad of a visually impaired reader and a sighted volunteer, or an individual expert proficient in both Chinese characters and Braille. This acute dependency on specialized human resources severely delays Braille literature production, stifling the timely supply of accessible learning materials and thereby impeding digital equity. To alleviate this persistent societal dilemma and promote inclusive learning design, this study developed a web-based assistive platform, Braille Reviser (B-Reviser). Bridging human empathy and algorithmic efficiency, B-Reviser empowers lay volunteers to independently correct Braille errors simply by modifying familiar Zhuyin (phonetic) symbols. Developed on a LAMP architecture, B-Reviser integrates the CNS11643 Full Character Library from Taiwan’s Government Open Data Platform to construct a robust character-to-phonetic baseline. To resolve the most intractable contextual ambiguities of polyphonic characters, B-Reviser leverages the Gemini Large Language Model for deep semantic analysis, substantially reducing transcription errors prior to human verification. Within the user interface, each Chinese character is rendered alongside its corresponding Zhuyin and Braille representations, with polyphonic characters visually highlighted to guide user attention. For any displayed character, clicking its Zhuyin displays all alternative pronunciations (as illustrated in Figure 1 below), while clicking the character itself links directly to an online Chinese dictionary for real-time reference. This workflow effectively dismantles the expertise barrier inherent in traditional proofreading, enabling lay volunteers to achieve precise correction autonomously. Ultimately, this human-centered proofreading platform addresses long-standing goals in assistive technology (Bhowmick & Hazarika, 2017). Preliminary evaluations demonstrate that B-Reviser significantly reduces technical thresholds, operational complexity, and task duration for volunteers. Centered on digital inclusion, this system exemplifies human-centric crowdsourcing design as a form of compassionate technology. Through human-artificial intelligence collaboration, B-Reviser empowers lay volunteers to accelerate the production of Braille literature, thereby promoting accessible learning and digital inclusion for individuals with visual impairments (Hersh & Johnson, 2008).

title: Trust, relationships and impact: Evidencing the human work of learning designers
abstractText: Learning designers (LDs) play a critical role in supporting higher education teaching and learning, especially through periods of significant digital change, from the rapid transition to online learning during COVID-19 to the redesign of learning and assessment in response to generative AI. In this increasingly digital and AI-enabled higher education sector, learning design is inherently relational, requiring practitioners to meet academics where they are and support educational change through trust, collaboration and compassion. Yet much of this work remains hidden, and difficult to articulate and demonstrate using traditional institutional measures. While output metrics such as consultations, workshops and resources developed provide evidence of activity, they often fail to capture the relational, collaborative and transformative nature of LD practice. Drawing on King and Patterson’s (2026) conception of course design as an act of care, we argue that many of the most significant contributions of LDs are relational rather than transactional. To address this challenge Boreland et al. (2025) developed the Learning Design Evidence Framework (LDEF) which provides a structured approach to evidencing the relational work underpinning educational innovation. The framework makes visible how LDs build trust, foster collaboration, influence practice, and create the conditions for meaningful educational change using seven segments; Student-Centered Design, Curriculum Design and Innovation, Professional Development, Promotion and Sharing of Quality Design, Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Leadership and Influence, and Recognition and Reward. Across each segment, meaningful impact is demonstrated through collaboration, partnership and sustained engagement with academics, students and institutional stakeholders. Together, the segments provide a structured approach to evidencing the breadth, depth and relational impact of LD practice. This interactive poster invites the ASCILITE community to inform what constitutes meaningful evidence of LD impact, drawing on diverse institutional contexts and practices across the sector. The poster itself is designed to be conversational, inviting delegates to contribute their perspectives by responding to three reflective prompts: What evidence do you think demonstrates the value of relationships and human connection in LD? What contributions of LDs have you noticed are often overlooked or invisible? What evidence do you see as most important in the future? Using pens and markers, or sticky notes, delegates will collectively build a visual representation of the evidence they value, the invisible work they recognise and the future directions they envision for the profession. This participatory approach reflects the framework’s emphasis on co-creation, reflective practice and shared understanding while creating opportunities for meaningful discussion among delegates from diverse institutional contexts. By the conclusion of the conference, the poster will have evolved into a collective representation of how the LD community values evidence, relationships, and impact. In doing so, it will demonstrate that the future of LD is not defined solely by digital technologies, but by the human connections that enable educational transformation.

title: Belonging through a web of connections in a first-year online course
abstractText: University learning, teaching and assessment is experiencing significant digital and pedagogical disruption. Accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, university teachers have experienced the shift to Emergency Remote Teaching, the increase of hybrid and online learning, followed by the rise of GenAI. These disruptions, combined with ramifications of neoliberalism and managerialism, have led to the erosion of connections and trust between students and teachers that have always been at the centre of learning and teaching. As such, knowing how to build and re-build connections with students is critical. Renewed research interest in the concept of belonging shows promise for re-building human connection in learning and teaching, however few studies have specifically focussed on belonging in post-pandemic online learning environments, especially within the first-year cohort. This qualitative case study examines one course including interviews with two teachers and three students, analysis of the course site, and observations of synchronous classes. Findings evidence that the teaching team humanised the online environment and directed academic belonging through place and social belonging by emphasising the learner-instructor relationship to facilitate student belonging.

title: Interatrial Septal Disorders are Independently Associated with Delayed Post-Exercise Heart Rate Recovery in Athletes
From nodal concordance to treatment selection: Does radiographic nodal count validate a TORS decision rule?
Exploring the Educational Landscape of Precision Agriculture Workforce Development in the United States
abstractText: As precision agriculture (PA) becomes increasingly important to agricultural production, secondary agricultural education must prepare teachers and students with skills needed for meaningful workforce participation. Guided by Human Capital Theory (HCT), this study synthesized peer-reviewed literature and publicly available curricula to examine the extent to which existing evidence and curriculum resources support teachers’ capacity and students’ readiness for participation in the PA workforce in the United States. A two-phase review design used deductive content analysis. Phase one was a PRISMA-informed scoping review of U.S.-based peer-reviewed studies, while phase two reviewed publicly available PA secondary school curricula. Eight studies and six curriculum resources met the inclusion criteria. Findings indicated that research in the area remains limited and has largely focused on short-term interventions. Although students often demonstrated increased confidence, knowledge, and career interest, teachers reported barriers such as limited professional development, weak curriculum guidance, and inadequate access to technology. Curriculum resources also varied considerably in accessibility, scope, and quality, and only one resource was standards-aligned. Overall, secondary PA education is building awareness and foundational skills, but it is not yet consistently preparing students for workforce participation. This review extends HCT by showing that current efforts build more general human capital than specific human capital needed for PA workforce readiness. This review emphasizes translating exposure into competence through an aligned curriculum, teacher capacity, and institutional support.

title: Designing inclusive interactive oral assessments: Practical learnings for educators
abstractText: As artificial intelligence continues to impact the higher education sector, Interactive Oral Assessments (IOAs) are increasingly used to assure assessment integrity. Whilst there are IOA best practice guidelines, there are concerns that the pace of implementation has compromised design, and considerations regarding student preparation, equity and inclusivity are being overlooked. This concise paper considers these issues through a case study of a postgraduate business subject and provides practical advice for how student preparation for oral tasks can be embedded within a curriculum without detracting from disciplinary knowledge and content. The design addressed five areas to support student IOA preparation: creating authentic scenarios; designing inclusive assessment practices for diverse cohorts; structured student preparation; balancing IOA preparation with course content coverage; and ensuring alignment between preparation activities and the actual IOA experience. Student feedback and educator observations suggest students felt increasingly prepared and supported throughout the semester. Recommendations are made for educators considering IOA including incorporation of low-stakes practice, creating classroom safety, setting clear expectations, preparing exemplars, focusing on student and educator preparation, and collaborating with others. This paper extends existing IOA literature by addressing inclusive practices for increasingly diverse student cohorts and contributes practical strategies for educators seeking to design IOA’s that support inclusion while balancing curriculum time and disciplinary content requirements.

title: Compensation Systems and Job Performance of Teaching Staff in Kenya Medical Training Colleges in Nakuru County, Kenya.
abstractText: Compensation systems are the financial and non-financial rewards that an employer provides in return for employees' contribution, and they are widely regarded as a central determinant of motivation, satisfaction and productivity, particularly in public institutions where standardized pay structures limit flexibility. Kenya Medical Training College (KMTC) has expanded rapidly in enrolment and campuses, yet regulatory audits point to staff shortages, high student–lecturer ratios and heavy workloads that threaten the job performance of teaching staff. The purpose of this study was therefore to examine the influence of compensation systems on the job performance of teaching staff in Kenya Medical Training Colleges in Nakuru County, Kenya. Specifically, the study examined the influence of staff allowances, performance-based incentives, employee benefits and non-financial rewards on job performance. The study was anchored on Equity Theory, Expectancy Theory, Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory and Total Rewards Theory. A descriptive research design was adopted, targeting 118 teaching staff in the Nakuru and Molo KMTC campuses. A sample of 92 respondents was determined using Yamane's formula and selected through proportionate stratified sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire, of which 90 were returned (97.8%), and were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The findings revealed that the four compensation dimensions jointly and significantly predicted job performance (F = 4.689, p = 0.002). Performance-based incentives had the strongest positive and significant influence on job performance (β = 0.297, p = 0.007), followed by non-financial rewards (β = 0.209, p = 0.041) and staff allowances (β = 0.115, p = 0.028), while employee benefits had a positive but statistically insignificant influence (β = 0.014, p = 0.896). The study concludes that rewards which are visibly linked to effort and recognition matter more for the performance of teaching staff than benefits that mainly provide security. The study recommends that KMTC management should institutionalize transparent performance-based reward and recognition mechanisms, periodically review the adequacy and equity of allowances and the compensation of overtime and additional duties, improve the management of leave entitlements, and sustain flexible work arrangements and work-life balance initiatives.

title: Rebalancing the algorithm: The educational technologist as an ecosystem custodian
abstractText: This paper is a conceptual position paper grounded in a decade of research into the values and beliefs of educational technologists (McNutt, 2019). It proposes that three interconnected concepts – Universal Design, ecosystem custodianship, and the poetic imagination offer a framework to inform and guide conversations and discussions on rebalancing the algorithm in the field of educational technology. The profession is standing at a crossroads as algorithmic systems are marginalising human judgement. There is an opportunity for educational technologists to assert their identity as ecosystem custodians – by cultivating environments where technological innovation, inclusive practice and human dignity remain in productive balance. The CONFRONT framework, originally presented at the EAN Conference (Craddock & McNutt, 2025) is anchored in eight poetic principles (Communicate, Opportunities, Nurture, Feel, Reduce, Ownership, Nudge, Trust), is proposed as a practical and philosophical architecture for that work. The paper’s one central argument, to quote Seamus Heaney, “If you have the words there is always a chance that you will find the way,” at its best, the algorithm should serve our poem, not the other way round.

title: Between risk and reform: Learning designers’ experiences of institutional responses to GenAI in assessment
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

title: Reading the cards: Rebalancing the algorithm in higher education
abstractText: Higher education continues to navigate uncertainty created by the emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Institutional responses have largely focused on assessment reform, educational integrity and governance. This conceptual paper frames GenAI as a wicked problem and considers institutional responses as acts of sensemaking through which universities establish shared understandings and guide actions. Drawing on tarot as an interpretive lens, we introduce eight archetypes as a conceptual framework for examining higher education’s response to GenAI. The archetypes were selected for their conceptual resonance with higher education’s response to GenAI, the productive tension between the traditional and shadow meanings, and their recognisable symbolism. Organised across three dimensions – encountering uncertainty, seeking certainty and rebalancing educational values – the framework traces readings from The Fool, The Magician, The Tower, through to The Emperor, Justice, to The High Priestess, The Lovers and The Star. This reading highlights the prominence of disruption, governance and regulation in current responses while bringing wisdom, relationships and hope clearly into view. We argue that rebalancing the algorithm requires educational values to guide GenAI integration. The framework offers an accessible way to surface different perspectives, support collective sensemaking and open dialogue about the educational futures being created.

title: Parameter effect analysis and optimization of a 10 W micro-free-piston Stirling generator
Revisiting educational foundations for learning in the age of Generative AI
abstractText: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has intensified discussions about assessment assurance, academic integrity, and graduate capability in higher education and vocational education and training (VET). Institutional responses have often prioritised assessment security, while a growing body of scholarship has sought to define the competencies required for AI literacy. This position paper argues that these developments, while important, risk overlooking longstanding educational traditions that remain highly relevant in AI-enabled learning environments. Drawing on critical literacy and Students-as-Partners scholarship, we contend that many capabilities now associated with AI literacy reflect enduring concerns regarding critical evaluation, ethical participation, and learner agency. Rather than proposing another AI-specific framework, we argue that established educational traditions provide a robust foundation for helping students engage with AI critically, ethically, and thoughtfully. We conclude by suggesting that educational responses to AI should prioritise critical dialogue and shared responsibility as students prepare for increasingly AI-enabled professional and social contexts.

title: Site conditions determine soil microbial responses to plant invasions in Natura 2000 habitats: evidence from wet meadows and riverside tall-herb vegetation
Designing simulation-based learning for international healthcare students in preparation of work-integrated learning
abstractText: International healthcare students experience additional stressors during mandated work-integrated learning (WIL), compared to domestic students. A key identified obstacle for international healthcare students can be the development of work-based relationships with healthcare staff and patients, due to language and culture differences (Hari et al., 2021; Oikarainen et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2023). Strategies to address these difficulties have included communication skills training (Brewer et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2016; Merry et al., 2021), accent-related communication (Chan et al., 2016) and cultural competence (Merry et al., 2021). While communication is critical, WIL incorporates many different physical, social and emotional learning components. A teaching method that encompasses contemporary learning theories, whilst capturing clinical and interpersonal skill development, is simulation-based learning (SBL) (Judd et al., 2023; Ludvig et al., 2024). SBL is widely used in healthcare training, however there are few comprehensive reviews of SBL approaches specifically for international healthcare students. This Pecha Kutcha presentation will present the process of designing a SBL intervention for nursing students, through a design-based research (DBR) framework.

title: High-quality genome assemblies of two dmy-deficient Oryzias curvinotus lineages reveal distinct sex-associated chromosomal regions
Contextual adaptation of the igroup presence questionnaire for manikin-based simulation: a structured expert review and feasibility pilot study
abstractText: Abstract Background Presence refers to a learner’s subjective sense of being within a simulated situation. Although presence may influence how learners engage with simulation, existing measures were developed primarily for virtual environments, and evidence supporting their use in manikin-based simulation is limited. We aimed to adapt an existing presence measure for use in manikin-based simulation and to assess whether it could be administered in routine simulation courses. Methods Twelve established presence and immersion questionnaires were identified through a targeted literature search; five were shortlisted and appraised against six predefined criteria by experts in a two-round structured review. The selected Igroup Presence Questionnaire was contextually adapted while retaining its 14-item format and proposed domain allocation. The adapted questionnaire was administered after an obstetric-emergencies course and a crisis resource management course. Responses were recorded on the original − 3 to + 3 scale, recoded to 0–6 for reporting, and summarized descriptively. Results The expert panel selected the Igroup Presence Questionnaire based on its length, reported measurement properties, availability of translations, and existing reference data. Most changes replaced terminology specific to virtual environments, although several items required more extensive rewording. Twenty of 34 course participants submitted questionnaire responses (58.8%): 9 of 18 in the obstetric-emergencies course and 11 of 16 in the crisis resource management course. Nineteen respondents answered all 14 items, while one omitted SP3. No spontaneous concerns about item wording were recorded, although clarity was not assessed formally. Spatial presence had the highest median score in both courses (obstetric emergencies: 3.40, IQR 3.05–3.75, n = 8; crisis resource management: 4.80, IQR 3.60–5.20, n = 11). No inferential between-course comparison was performed. Conclusions The adapted questionnaire could be administered in two manikin-based simulation courses. This pilot does not establish the validity or reliability of the adapted instrument or support comparisons between courses. Cognitive interviews with intended respondents and evaluation in a larger, multicenter sample are required before the scores can be used to evaluate simulation design.

title: Autonomia controlada e controle autônomo: um modelo da relação treinador-atleta
abstractText: Sports team coach leadership has always been admired by society, and has proven a valuable case-study for various other contexts. It plays a crucial role in player and team performance. Over the last years, several studies have taken an ecological approach towards sports teams, bringing forward several questions concerning the coach’s modus operandi and the interactions among coach, team, athlete and game environment. Understanding the relation between autonomy and control is of paramount importance to the achievement of better performances. The present conceptual study examines how a coach may promote his players’ and team’s autonomy without relinquishing control over them.

title: From prompt to practice: A visual framework for AI-supported creative learning in animation education
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students imagine, produce, revise and communicate creative work. In animation education, AI tools can support rapid ideation, visual experimentation and alternative design pathways, but they also raise questions about how students continue to develop foundational skills, creative judgement, peer critique and reflective practice. This poster presents a classroom-informed visual framework for integrating AI into practice-based creative learning without reducing learning to prompt generation or final outputs. The framework was developed through practice-led curriculum redesign in an undergraduate animation course. It is informed by reflective practice, foundational animation principles, authentic learning, engagement theory and recent debates about AI in higher education (Bearman et al., 2023; Herrington, 2006; Kearsley & Shneiderman, 1998; Schön, 1983; Thomas & Johnston, 1981). Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for craft, critique or student decision-making, the framework maps AI-supported creative learning as an iterative studio process: observe, experiment, generate, critique, reflect, refine and share. This cycle visualises how AI can be embedded within classroom activities while keeping human judgement, feedback, revision and ethical decision-making central to learning. The poster focuses on how this framework can support creative practice in the classroom. It highlights how students may use AI to explore visual possibilities, test ideas, compare alternatives and reflect on their decisions, while still being assessed on process, reasoning, feedback use, authorship and responsible tool engagement. The visual model is organised around four pedagogical commitments: reflection; iteration; collaboration and critique; and ethical decision-making. By foregrounding a practical classroom case and a visual teaching framework, this poster contributes to ASCILITE 2026’s themes of connection, collaboration, creativity and compassion in a digital society. Although grounded in animation education, the model offers transferable strategies for educators designing AI-supported learning in creative, project-based and practice-based courses.

title: Designing together: Using a boundary object to support collaborative unit design conversations
abstractText: Designing learning experiences in higher education requires the negotiation of multiple priorities; aligning learning outcomes, teaching activities, assessment design, student workload, academic integrity, accreditation requirements, and implementation feasibility (Bearman et al., 2016). Yet, these considerations are often distributed across documents, systems, and stakeholders, making it difficult to develop a shared understanding of a unit as an integrated learning experience (Bearman et al., 2016). Visual learning design representations can make pedagogical decisions explicit and support communication and reflection between academics and designers (Agostinho, 2011; Conole et al., 2013) This Pecha Kucha explores the use of a visual consultation board using Miro at The University of Western Australia. The approach originated during the collaborative redesign of a unit, where two Learning and Assessment Designers and a Unit Coordinator mapped the assessment sequence as part of the student learning journey. The board connected the cadence of learning activities and assessments, feedback opportunities, student and staff workload, and relationships between tasks into a shared visual structure. Iterative conversations around the board informed changes to unit design. Reflection on this case study and feedback from the Unit Coordinator informed further refinement and adaptations of the board for consultations in other disciplinary contexts. While the board began as a visual learning design representation, the presentation analyses how it became a boundary object through collaborative knowledge practices of those using it. Drawing on the concept of boundary objects (Carlile, 2002; Star & Griesemer, 1989), we argue that the significance of the board lies not simply in being digital, visual or adaptable, but in how collaborators used and changed the shared representation. Academic and professional collaborators made assumptions visible, developed a shared vocabulary for discussing unit design, negotiated priorities and revised the representation in response. Following Damsa and Muukonen’s (2019) conception of shared knowledge objects as evolving through participant interaction, and consistent with Morrison et al.’s (2025) analysis of how boundary objects reshape meaning, language and practice across professional contexts, we contend that the board’s boundary-object function emerged through collaborative interpretation, material revision, consequential design change and adaptation through subsequent consultations, allowing shared understandings to be established, revisited and reworked over time. By tracing the development of the board, this session highlights the role of visual representations in supporting communication across academic and professional boundaries and considers how shared design artefacts can facilitate more coherent, intentional and collaborative approaches to curriculum design, especially among staff who may not share the same pedagogical expertise or terminology. This Pecha Kucha offers practical insights into how visual learning design representations can support richer conversations about curriculum design by helping academics and professional staff discuss, negotiate, and align competing aspects of learning design. In increasingly complex educational environments, attendees will see how shared design artefacts can strengthen academic-professional partnerships, support more coherent and intentional decision-making, and enable successive curriculum conversations to build on, rather than restart, previous interpretations, decisions and design revisions.

title: PENGARUH EDUKASI PEMILIHAN MENU MAKANAN DENGAN BOOKLET DAN DEMONSTRASI TERHADAP PENGETAHUAN IBU HAMIL TENTANG PROTEIN
abstractText: ABSTRACT Adequate protein intake during pregnancy plays an important role in supporting maternal health and fetal development. However, limited knowledge regarding the selection of protein sources may hinder pregnant women in choosing appropriate daily meals, particularly those experiencing nutritional problems. This study aimed to analyze changes in pregnant women's knowledge of protein following dietary menu selection education delivered through a booklet and demonstration. A quantitative approach with a pre-experimental design using a one-group pretest–posttest model was employed. A total of 46 pregnant women experiencing Chronic Energy Deficiency (CED), anemia, or both conditions in the working area of Plosoklaten Community Health Center were recruited using total sampling. Data were collected through questionnaires, and differences in knowledge before and after the intervention were analyzed using the Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test. The results showed that the proportion of respondents with good knowledge increased from 76.1% at baseline to 95.7% following the educational intervention. Statistical analysis indicated a significant difference, with a p-value of p < 0.001. These findings suggest that education using booklets and demonstrations was associated with improved knowledge of protein among pregnant women. The combination of these methods may serve as an alternative approach to delivering nutrition education in maternal healthcare services. ABSTRAK Pemenuhan kebutuhan protein selama kehamilan berperan dalam mendukung kesehatan ibu dan perkembangan janin. Namun, keterbatasan pengetahuan mengenai pemilihan sumber protein dapat menjadi kendala dalam menentukan menu makanan yang sesuai, terutama pada ibu hamil dengan masalah gizi. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis perubahan pengetahuan ibu hamil tentang protein setelah memperoleh edukasi pemilihan menu makanan melalui media booklet dan demonstrasi. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain pre-experimental melalui pola one-group pretest–posttest. Sebanyak 46 ibu hamil yang mengalami Kekurangan Energi Kronis (KEK), anemia, atau kedua kondisi tersebut di wilayah kerja Puskesmas Plosoklaten dilibatkan sebagai responden menggunakan teknik total sampling. Pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui kuesioner, sedangkan analisis perbedaan pengetahuan sebelum dan sesudah intervensi menggunakan Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa proporsi responden dengan pengetahuan baik meningkat dari 76,1% pada pengukuran awal menjadi 95,7% setelah edukasi. Hasil pengujian statistik menunjukkan perbedaan yang signifikan dengan nilai p < 0,001. Temuan ini mengindikasikan bahwa edukasi menggunakan booklet dan demonstrasi berkaitan dengan peningkatan pengetahuan ibu hamil tentang protein. Kombinasi kedua metode tersebut berpotensi dimanfaatkan sebagai alternatif penyampaian edukasi gizi dalam pelayanan kesehatan ibu hamil.

title: Fabrication of Vitamin E-Loaded Rhamnolipid Nanoemulsion for Antioxidant and Selective-Cleansing Applications
abstractText: Abstract With the growing demand for mild precision skincare, conventional synthetic surfactant-based facial cleansers nonselectively strip both sebum triglycerides (TG) and skin-barrier lipids (ceramides, cholesterol), resulting in barrier impairment, skin dryness, and oxidative damage. Biosurfactant rhamnolipid (Rha) exhibits amphiphilic properties, yet pure Rha nanocarriers suffer from poor colloidal stability and limited antioxidant protection. In this work, we aimed to construct pea-protein-isolate-stabilized Rha nanoemulsion (Rha-PPI-HS-VE) for vitamin E (VE) delivery, achieving dual functions of UV-oxidative-stress protection and lipid-selective cleansing. The pH-shift-treated unfolded pea-protein isolate (PPI) was assembled with rhamnolipid, using hemisqualane (HS) as an oil core to solubilize VE. After process optimization, a monodisperse nanoemulsion was obtained with particle size of 108.5 nm, polydispersity index (PDI) of 0.128, and a high VE encapsulation efficiency (EE) of 99.73 ± 0.03%. In vitro assays showed that 10% sample achieved 63.91% DPPH and 88.20% ABTS radical-scavenging rates (SR) and retained most antioxidant activity after 90-day storage. In UVB-damaged HaCaT keratinocytes, Rha-PPI-HS-VE (0.32%) markedly alleviated oxidative stress (the intracellular fluorescence of reactive-oxygen-species (ROS) probe decreased from 11,340 to 4722) and restored mitochondrial membrane potential. When incorporated into cleansing formulation, the nanoemulsion removed up to 86.16% triglyceride while preserving ceramides and cholesterol without significant loss. This study demonstrates that PPI-Rha biopolymer nanoemulsion can serve as a multifunctional green carrier, offering technical support for developing next-generation mild cleansing cosmetic raw materials with antioxidant-repair and selective-lipid-regulating functions.

title: A proposal for a student-centred framework for critical thinking with Generative AI in mathematics education
abstractText: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping mathematics education by providing students with immediate access to explanations, worked examples, and problem-solving support. While these capabilities offering opportunities to enrich learning, they also raise concerns about how students develop critical thinking when AI-generated solutions are readily available. The use of GenAI is increasing in Bhutanese schools but little is known about how teachers and students currently use these technologies in mathematics classrooms or what pedagogical challenges limit their effective integration. This conceptual paper proposes a mixed-methods study to identify the opportunities, challenges, and pedagogical gaps associated with the use of GenAI in mathematics education, using Bhutanese secondary schools as the study context. Guided by a pragmatic paradigm, the study will employ questionnaires with quantitative and qualitative components to explore current practices, perceptions, and experiences of teachers and students. The findings will inform the development of a contextually relevant pedagogical framework that positions GenAI as a cognitive scaffold for analysing mathematical problems, evaluating alternative solution strategies, and strengthening critical thinking. By establishing an evidence base before framework design, the proposed study aims to support the responsible integration of GenAI into mathematics education and provide direction for future research, curriculum development, and classroom practice.
